title: Area VII review: Slow Flight and Stalls
intro: These questions mix all five Tasks of Area VII: slow flight, power-off, power-on and accelerated stalls, and spin awareness. Many join two Tasks in one flight, the way the examiner strings them together on the checkride.

questions.q: On one checkride flight you will fly slow flight, a power-off stall and an accelerated stall over the same practice area. The highest terrain there is 1,400 ft MSL. What are the lowest altitudes at which each Task may be completed?
options: 2,900 ft MSL for all three Tasks, since every Area VII Task has the same 1,500 ft AGL floor there
2,900 ft MSL for slow flight and the power-off stall; 4,400 ft MSL for the accelerated stall
1,500 ft MSL for slow flight and for the power-off stall; 3,000 ft MSL for the accelerated stall
4,400 ft MSL for slow flight; 2,900 ft MSL for both stalls, since slow flight needs the higher floor
questions.why: Slow flight and the power-off stall must be completed no lower than 1,500 ft AGL in a single-engine airplane (ACS CA.VII.A.S2, CA.VII.B.S2). The accelerated stall must be completed no lower than 3,000 ft AGL (ACS CA.VII.D.S2). Add the terrain: 1,400 + 1,500 = 2,900 ft MSL and 1,400 + 3,000 = 4,400 ft MSL. The 1,500 and 3,000 ft MSL answer forgets that the floors are above the ground, not above sea level. Plan your entry higher still, so the altitude the recovery uses fits above the floor [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

questions.q: The examiner asks for a turning power-off stall with 20 degrees of bank, and later a turning power-on stall with 20 degrees of bank. Both times your bank drifts to 27 degrees before the stall. How does each one score?
options: The power-off stall fails and the power-on stall passes
Both fail, since 27 degrees is more than the 20 degree limit
The power-off stall passes and the power-on stall fails
Both pass, since both Tasks allow plus or minus 10 degrees of bank
questions.why: The power-off stall allows the specified bank plus or minus 5 degrees, so 15 to 25 degrees (ACS CA.VII.B.S6). The power-on stall allows plus or minus 10 degrees, so 10 to 30 degrees (ACS CA.VII.C.S6). 27 degrees is outside the first window and inside the second. 'Both fail' is tempting, but the 20 degree figure limits the bank the examiner may specify; the tolerance is then added to that specified bank. Application: the two Tasks look alike, so fly both to the tighter power-off window.

questions.q: In landing-configuration slow flight the stall horn starts and keeps sounding. It is not a short chirp from a bump. What has happened, and what is your first action?
options: You are still in slow flight; hold the attitude and add power until the horn stops
You are in a full stall; add full power first to limit the altitude you will lose
You have reached an impending stall; reduce the AOA until the warning stops
You are in a secondary stall; level the wings first, then lower the nose and add power
questions.why: Slow flight must be flown without a stall warning (ACS CA.VII.A.S4). An impending stall is when the AOA sets off a stall warning but has not reached the critical AOA; a full stall is when the critical AOA is exceeded [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. The first step is to reduce the AOA until the stall warning is gone [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Adding power first is wrong: pilots who put power and altitude first have lost control, and power alone does not end a stall [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. The turbulence allowance covers only a momentary horn that you recognize and correct promptly (ACS CA.VII.A, Appendix 3).

questions.q: Before the checkride you review which configuration the examiner may ask for in three Tasks. Which matches the commercial ACS?
options: Slow flight: landing only. Power-off stall: approach or landing. Power-on stall: takeoff only
Slow flight: as the evaluator specifies. Power-off stall: approach or landing. Power-on stall: takeoff, departure or cruise
Slow flight: as the evaluator specifies. Power-off stall: cruise or landing. Power-on stall: takeoff or approach
All three: any configuration the evaluator names
questions.why: Slow flight is flown with the airplane configured as specified by the evaluator (ACS CA.VII.A.S4). It is typically evaluated in the landing configuration, but clean or takeoff configurations may also be evaluated [[24:116|AFH 5-11]], so 'landing only' is wrong. The power-off stall uses the approach or landing configuration (ACS CA.VII.B.S3). The power-on stall uses the takeoff, departure or cruise configuration (ACS CA.VII.C.S3). 'Any configuration' is wrong because the two stall Tasks each name their own list.

questions.q: Your airplane meets current Part 23, so it must have no tendency to inadvertently depart controlled flight. A fellow student says that means he can be loose with the rudder in slow flight turns. What is the best reply?
options: He is right; a Part 23 airplane cannot spin unless the pilot deliberately holds full pro-spin controls for turns
He is right for slow flight, since the stall warning will always protect you there, but not for power-on stalls
Wrong: reluctant to spin is not spin-proof; uncoordinated slow flight can still cause an accidental spin
Wrong, but only because the commercial ACS tolerance for the ball is tighter than the Part 23 requirement
questions.why: Part 23 does require that single-engine airplanes not certified for aerobatics have no tendency to inadvertently depart controlled flight [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]]. But the AFH says modern airplanes are more reluctant to spin, not unable to: mishandling the controls in turns, stalls and uncoordinated slow flight can put even the most reluctant airplane into an accidental spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. The primary cause of an inadvertent spin is exceeding the critical AOA with too much or too little rudder [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]]. The 'tighter ACS rule' option is wrong because the ACS gives no separate ball tolerance; it asks for coordinated flight (ACS CA.VII.A.S4).

questions.q: In slow flight your CFI asks you to work out true airspeed with your flight computer, then to find a heading to an airport on the chart. Why does the FAA want this kind of training?
options: It keeps your eyes inside the cockpit, which the AFH says is the best way to hold airspeed
The commercial ACS requires a true airspeed calculation and a heading to be worked during slow flight
Flight computer work helps you trim the airplane for the slow-flight speed more precisely
NTSB data show most stall/spin accidents follow a momentary distraction from flying
questions.why: AC 61-67C says NTSB statistics show most stall/spin accidents result when a pilot is distracted momentarily from flying, which is why realistic distractions were added to flight test maneuvers [[13:4|AC 61-67C para 3]]. It lists distractions at low airspeed such as computing true airspeed or finding a heading on a chart, with attention divided between the task and flying [[13:16|AC 61-67C para 200a(10)]]. No ACS element asks for a true airspeed calculation (ACS CA.VII.A). Keeping your eyes inside is wrong: fixation on the instruments is a listed slow flight error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

questions.q: On the checkride the examiner will tell you how far to take each stall. In which Tasks may the examiner ask you to go to a full stall?
options: All three stall Tasks, power-off, power-on and accelerated, whenever the evaluator asks for a full stall
Only the accelerated stall, since it is the commercial-only Task and so needs the most proof
Power-off and power-on stalls only; the accelerated stall goes only to an impending stall
None; commercial stalls always recover at the first indication, and a full stall is never flown
questions.why: For both the power-off and the power-on stall you recover at the first indication or after a full stall, as the evaluator specifies (ACS CA.VII.B.S8, CA.VII.C.S8). In the accelerated stall you increase back pressure until an impending stall is reached, then acknowledge the first cue and recover (ACS CA.VII.D.S5 to S7). 'All three' is the tempting mistake because the accelerated stall is the Task only commercial and flight instructor applicants are asked to fly [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

questions.q: Before a series of power-off stalls, your ADS-B In display shows no traffic below you. You are tempted to skip the clearing turns. What does the AIM say?
options: Skip them; ADS-B In shows all traffic around you, so clearing turns are only for airplanes without it
Clear anyway: not every aircraft shows on ADS-B In, and clearing should come before every stall
Skip them below 3,000 ft AGL, where ADS-B coverage is best and the display shows everything nearby
Clear only the area above you, since the display already covers all of the airspace below your altitude
questions.why: The AIM calls ADS-B In an effective aid, but in certain airspace not every aircraft has ADS-B Out or a transponder, so some will not appear on the display [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]]. Clearing procedures should come before stalls, slow flight and other maneuvers [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f]], and the commercial ACS asks you to clear the area (ACS CA.VII.B.S1). 'Clear only above' gets it backwards: before a stall the area at and below your altitude matters most, because the maneuver descends [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

questions.q: A safety seminar speaker quotes accident numbers for stalls and spins. Which statement matches the PHAK?
options: Stall/spin accidents happen mostly in the cruise phase, so the approach and landing are the safest phases of flight
Engine failure is the top cause of fatal accidents, and stall/spin causes only about 10 percent of maneuvering ones
Loss of control is only a minor cause of fatalities, and 26.6 percent of maneuvering-phase fatal accidents involve stall/spin
Loss of control is the top cause of fatalities, and about half of maneuvering fatal accidents involve stall/spin
questions.why: The PHAK says loss of control is the number one root cause of fatalities in general and commercial aviation. More than 25 percent of GA fatal accidents occur in the maneuvering phase, and half of those involve stall/spin scenarios [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]]. The 26.6 percent figure is real but means something else: AC 90-48E gives it as the share of all fatal accidents in the last 10 years that happened during maneuvering flight [[16:12|AC 90-48E 11.2.2.1]].

questions.q: In a straight-ahead power-off full stall you hold the yoke full aft. While glancing at the altimeter you let your left foot push the rudder hard as the stall breaks. Why does the AFH compare this to a spin entry?
options: It does not; a power-off stall cannot become a spin because the power is at idle
The AFH spin entry is a power-off stall with full rudder toward the rotation and full back elevator at the stall, so you have supplied both stall and yaw
Only aileron can start a spin; rudder alone just yaws the nose
Left rudder at idle power cancels P-factor, so the airplane stays coordinated
questions.why: The AFH says the entry for a spin demonstration is like a power-off stall: power to idle, nose up to a stalling attitude, then full rudder toward the desired rotation with full back elevator as the stall approaches [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. A spin needs a stalled wing plus yaw or sideslip at the stall [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Idle power does not prevent it, and wrong rudder is one of the yaw sources, along with adverse yaw from aileron [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Reduce the AOA and use rudder to stop the yaw [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

questions.q: You plan power-on stalls with a non-pilot friend aboard. No instructor is on board and it is not a flight test. On one entry you raise the nose to 35 degrees above the horizon. What does that mean under 14 CFR 91.307?
options: Nothing; the rule covers only bank angles over 60 degrees
It was not allowed unless every occupant was wearing an approved parachute, since the nose-up attitude exceeded 30 degrees
Only you need a parachute, as pilot in command
Nothing; stall practice is always exempt from the parachute rule
questions.why: With anyone other than a crewmember aboard, no pilot may make an intentional maneuver that exceeds 60 degrees of bank or 30 degrees nose-up or nose-down unless each occupant wears an approved parachute [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]]. The exceptions are flight tests for a certificate or rating, and spins and other required maneuvers given by a CFI or an ATP instructing under 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]]. Neither applies here, so 'always exempt' is wrong. The AFH notes that power-on stalls can reach a very high nose-up attitude unless the airplane is slowed first, and some manufacturers limit the pitch to 30 degrees [[24:347|AFH 17-13]]. So slow down first, and plan the entry to stay at or below 30 degrees with a passenger aboard.

questions.q: A thunderstorm sits near the departure end. Your passenger says, 'If we hit a microburst we can just fly a stall recovery.' What do the FAA sources say about the time you would have?
options: About 5 to 15 minutes, the usual life of a microburst, which gives plenty of time to react
About a minute, which is enough time for a normal power-on stall recovery and a go-around
About 20 seconds, after which the outflow is always behind you and you are safely clear of it
Only 5 to 15 seconds may be available to respond, and some microbursts cannot be escaped
questions.why: The AWH says only 5 to 15 seconds may be available to recognize and respond to a wind shear encounter [[28:269|AWH 22-14]], and that some microbursts cannot be escaped with any known technique [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. In the takeoff accidents studied, the takeoff looked normal for 5 seconds and the airplane crashed about 20 seconds after lift-off [[28:266|AWH 22-11]], so 20 seconds is no safe point. 5 to 15 minutes is a microburst's usual lifespan [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]], not your reaction time. The defense is not to depart into one.

questions.q: You fly a low-wing airplane. Before a power-on stall in a right climbing turn, how does the AIM say to clear in the direction of the turn?
options: Momentarily lower the right wing and look
Momentarily raise the right wing and look
Raise the nose to the stall attitude first, then look under the wings
Rely on the high nose attitude, since it gives the best view ahead
questions.why: In a low-wing airplane the AIM says to momentarily lower the wing in the direction of the intended turn and look; raising the wing is the high-wing method [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f]]. Clearing should come before stalls and climbs [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f]]. The aircraft attitude itself creates extra blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]], so clear before you raise the nose, not after.

questions.q: On a cold morning you find a thin layer of frost on the wings before a short-field departure. A passenger says, 'It's barely there, and the stall horn will warn us if it matters.' What is correct?
options: Fly, but climb 5 knots faster than VX to cover the higher stall speed, since the horn will warn you
Fly; frost only matters in flight, where it adds a little weight, and the takeoff roll will clear it
Remove it first: even a little raises the stall speed, and a stall may come with little warning
Fly, since frost changes only the true airspeed of the stall, not the indicated airspeed you will fly
questions.why: Even a small amount of snow, ice or frost changes the wing's shape, raises the stall speed, adds drag and cuts lift, and flight should not be attempted with it on the surfaces [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100k]]. As little as 0.8 millimeter of ice on the upper wing surface reduces lift by 25 percent [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]]. With icing, a stall may come with little or none of the usual cues, such as buffet or the stall horn [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 102a]]. Adding speed is wrong because the AC says not to fly at all, not to fly faster.

questions.q: You just finished a full-flap power-off stall. The examiner says, 'Now an accelerated stall, your choice of configuration.' What do you set, and why?
options: Leave full flaps, since a lower stall speed keeps the loads lower
Flaps up, since the ACS lets the accelerated stall be flown only clean
Half flaps, as a compromise between stall speed and loads
Flaps up, since the design G limits are lower with flaps extended
questions.why: The AFH says never to practice accelerated stalls with the flaps extended, because the design G-load limits are lower in that configuration [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. The ACS itself only says to set the configuration the evaluator specifies (ACS CA.VII.D.S3), so the 'only clean' answer gives the wrong reason. Flaps do lower the stall speed [[13:7|AC 61-67C para 100c]], but in this Task you deliberately load the wing above 1 G, so the lower flap G limit is what matters.

questions.q: You just finished a power-on stall at the 65 percent power the ACS asks for. The examiner says, 'Now a power-on accelerated stall, clean.' What power standard applies to this Task?
options: No less than 65 percent power, the same minimum that applies to the power-on stall Task you just flew
Idle only, since the ACS allows accelerated stalls only with the power at idle, never power-on
Power appropriate for the configuration, so airspeed stays within VA and other POH/AFM limits
Full power, so you can hold altitude and keep the airspeed up through the 45 degree banked turn
questions.why: The accelerated stall Task covers power-on or power-off entries, and asks you to set power appropriate for the configuration so the airspeed does not exceed VA or any other POH/AFM limit (ACS CA.VII.D.S4). The 65 percent minimum belongs to the power-on stall Task only (ACS CA.VII.C.S4), so carrying it over is the trap: it can push you past VA. The AFH agrees: never fly the accelerated stall faster than the manufacturer's recommended speed, VA or VO [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Above VA the airplane can reach its design load limit before the critical AOA [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

questions.q: After an accelerated stall recovery you are at 95 knots, below the airplane's 105-knot VA. A friend says, 'Below VA you can't hurt it, so slam in full aileron and full back elevator together to get level fast.' What is the correct reply?
options: Correct, because anywhere below VA the airplane is protected against any combination of control inputs
Correct, as long as the airspeed stays below VA during the whole pull and the loads stay under limits
Wrong, but only because VA rises as weight drops, so the 95 knots you are flying is above the new VA
Wrong: being below VA does not protect against full inputs in more than one axis at the same time
questions.why: At or below VA a single full control deflection reaches the stall before the design limit load [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. But the PHAK says operating below VA does not protect against multiple full inputs in one axis or full inputs in more than one axis at once [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]], and AC 61-67C warns that rapid, large alternating inputs combined with big pitch, roll or yaw changes can break the airplane even below VA [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100f]]. The weight answer has VA backward: maneuvering speed is lower at a lower weight [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100l]].

questions.q: In a left turning power-off stall you let the ball slide out by holding too much left rudder with your left aileron, a skid. The left wing drops at the stall and rotation starts. Which way is the spin, and which rudder does the AFH template call for after power idle and ailerons neutral?
options: Left spin; full right rudder
Right spin; full left rudder
Left spin; full left rudder to stay coordinated
Right spin, opposite the aileron; full right rudder
questions.why: In a skidding turn, with aileron and rudder applied the same way, the spin rotates in the direction the controls are applied, here to the left [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]]. A stall in a skid or slip spins in the direction of the rudder, whichever wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. The template is power idle, ailerons neutral, then full rudder opposite the rotation, so full right rudder [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. 'Opposite the aileron' is the rule for a slip, not a skid [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

questions.q: On a dual flight in a spin-approved airplane, your CFI has you enter an incipient spin to the right. Your plan: let it make one full turn so you are sure of the direction, then ease in left rudder gently so you don't overcontrol. What is wrong with that plan?
options: Nothing; gentle rudder prevents a secondary spin
Only the rudder; waiting a full turn is right so you can use the ball for direction
Only the timing; once you start, gentle rudder is correct
Both: start incipient spin recovery before 360 degrees of rotation, and apply the rudder briskly and fully, since slow, cautious rudder can let it keep spinning
questions.why: The AFH says to begin incipient spin recovery before 360 degrees of rotation, with full rudder opposite the rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Rudder is usually the most important recovery control in single-engine airplanes, applied briskly and fully; slow, overly cautious rudder can let the airplane spin indefinitely, even with anti-spin inputs [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. The ball is no guide to direction, since its movement depends on where the instrument is mounted; use the turn indicator [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

questions.q: A stall recovery and a spin recovery both use forward elevator. Which statement fits what the sources teach?
options: In a stall, use just enough, since too much forward pressure puts a negative load on the wing; in a spin, the AFH template calls for positive, brisk forward elevator, forward of neutral, sometimes full forward
In both, just relax back pressure; forward of neutral is never needed
In both, push to the forward stop, since more forward pressure always breaks the stall faster
In a stall, push to the stop; in a spin, keep the elevator neutral until the rotation stops
questions.why: Every airplane needs a different amount of forward pressure or relaxation of back pressure to recover from a stall, and too much forward pressure can hinder recovery by imposing a negative load on the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 105]]. In a spin, the AFH template step is positive, brisk, straight-forward elevator, forward of neutral, right after the full rudder, and in some cases full forward elevator is needed [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Some airplanes need only a relaxation of back pressure in spin recovery and others full forward, which is why the POH comes first [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]] [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

questions.q: A four-seat airplane is approved for spins in the utility category. Last week it recovered cleanly from spins with you and your CFI aboard. Today you add two rear passengers and bags; the CG is aft of the utility limit but inside the normal-category limit. What do the sources say?
options: The airplane enters spins more easily and may not recover from one that goes beyond one turn; a CG one or two inches further aft can make normal recovery inputs fail
Spins are fine if you start recovery before the second turn
The heavier airplane is more spin-resistant, since weight raises the stall speed
Spins are fine, since the airplane is still within a certified CG limit
questions.why: The utility-category aft CG limit for spins is usually several inches forward of the normal-category limit [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]. An airplane approved for spins in the utility category but loaded to normal-category limits can have less resistance to spin entry and may not recover from a spin that goes beyond one turn [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. An airplane that recovers cleanly at one CG may fail completely to respond to normal recovery attempts with the CG one or two inches further aft [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]. 'Within a certified limit' is the trap: extra aft weight can stay within CG and still seriously affect spin recovery [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
